messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 48

It begins forty-two years ago in a crowded market square. He is twenty-nine, traveling with a colleague for a restoration project. The day starts ordinary. The smell of roasting spices, the chatter of vendors, the weight of canvas bags on his shoulders. Then the air fractures. The ground jumps. Shrapnel cuts through the noise, turning shouts into silence. He runs. The smoke burns his throat. He reaches for his colleague’s hand and finds only empty air. When the dust settles, he is alone in a street of shattered glass and stillness. He does not speak of it. He packs his brushes and goes home. The years that follow fold into a routine of quiet survival. He returns to painting, his hands moving across stretched canvas with mechanical precision. He tells himself he must keep working, that creation is the only anchor left. But the past does not stay buried. It waits in the periphery. When doors slam, his breath stops. When a car backfires, his shoulders hike to his ears. He stops going to the market. He stops answering his phone. He begins to measure his life in distances: how far he sleeps from the street, how many locks he turns, how many windows he avoids looking through. His apartment grows sparse. He orders food online. He sleeps with the chair braced against the door, waking before dawn with his heart racing, certain the walls are closing in again. The dreams come unbidden. They never show the explosion. They show the running. They show the reaching. They end with him sitting upright, gasping, as the morning light confirms he is still here. He paints to keep the quiet at bay. The studio becomes his territory. He mixes pigments with deliberate care, layering glazes over linen, scraping away what doesn’t fit. He tells clients the paint needs time to breathe, that rushing ruins the work. He applies the same rule to himself. He watches the clock. He eats alone. He hums old work songs from his Oceania heritage when the air grows too thick, the rhythms grounding him when the present feels sharp. He does not date. He does not make new friends. He outlives the places that once mattered. The world moves forward, loud and unbothered. He stays still. Now, at seventy-one, he sits before an unfinished seascape. His hands are mapped with fine lines and dried pigment, the knuckles stiff from decades of holding brushes. He pauses when a siren wails through the street. His fingers go cold. The smell of burnt paper drifts through the crack in his window. He counts to three. He forces his shoulders down. He picks up the brush. He mixes a darker blue. The street outside grows quiet. He lifts the brush and continues.
